title: Kernel Guild: adaptive selector for token-phase & compute-characteristic aware scheduling
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Current runtime picks kernels primarily on static heuristics (arch family + avg seqlen buckets) which misses token-phase effects (prefill vs. decode) and transient compute characteristics (chiplet occupancy, burst contention). Goal: build a lightweight adaptive selector — the 'Kernel Guild' — that groups compatible kernels into guilds and selects between them with an online bandit informed by token-phase, recent seqlen histogram, and short-term microbenchmarks. The selector should be safe for production canaries and provide measurable P50/P95 latency and cost improvements with minimal regression risk.
background_and_rationale: We observed ~12% P95 regression on mixed prefill/decode workloads when using a single kernel per model family for heterogeneous GPU types. Prior approaches (full bandit over kernel space per-request) add too much probe traffic. Guilds let us reduce exploration space, warm-start with offline microbenchmarks, and route with token-phase-aware priors. This complements recent work on KV cache and batching optimizations by reducing compute tail latency without changing request batching semantics.
benchmarks: Local microbench harness: guild_v0_baseline.csv (prefill-heavy, decode-heavy, mixed) - p50/p95 token latency
acceptance_criteria: Selector reduces mean inference cost per token by >=5% on mixed workloads in simulated traffic
No more than 2% increase in P95 latency for any major customer workload during 2-week canary
Graceful fallback: when a guild candidate fails microprobe or exceeds safety threshold, runtime falls back to verified default kernel with zero request drops
Automated telemetry visible in Console: per-route kernel distribution, regret metric, probe rate

decisions_and_tradeoffs: Tradeoff: probing fewer candidates (guild-level) reduces exploration cost but risks missing rare high-performance microkernels. Chosen: prioritize low probe rate + periodic re-evaluation windows.

Decision: Use token-phase (prefill/decode) as primary routing feature; per-request seqlen bucket is secondary. Rationale: token-phase correlates strongly with memory access pattern and KV cache usage.
Tradeoff: Online bandit with Thompson sampling vs. epsilon-greedy. Chosen Thompson sampling for faster convergence on scarce probe signals but added conservatism via safety thresholds.
implementation_notes: Guild registry persisted in config service with optimistic concurrency to allow remote tuning.
Microprobe harness runs O(3) short-run kernels per guild candidate; probe scheduling uses token-phase-aware cooldowns.
Telemetry emits per-guild counters: probes, wins, average_latency, cost_delta, probe_rate, regret_estimate.
Fallbacks: circuit-breaker trips after X consecutive probe failures or Y% regression observed in the last N minutes (configurable).
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: probe traffic causes transient tail latency spikes. Mitigation: low probe budget, phase-aware scheduling, and synthetic probe piggybacking during low-util windows.
Risk: inaccurate microbench results on shared noisy hosts. Mitigation: aggregate over multiple microprobes and prefer hardware-topology-aware probes.
Risk: cold-start for new GPUs/models. Mitigation: warmstart using offline microbench corpus and cross-arch transfer priors.
rollback_plan: Disable kernel guild selector via runtime feature flag (console toggle) — immediate route to default kernel.
If P95 regression > 2% observed in canary: pause probes, revert routing to pinned kernel, and run postmortem within 48h.
